unit.unitOverview: Stop looking words up. Split an unfamiliar word at its prefix and work it out. Form a negative with the right prefix and the right doubled letter. visual.lectureScript:
Welcome to Stage 8. From here to the end of Unit 14 you are working at B1, which means longer sentences, denser writing, and more of it read rather than spoken.
This unit is the one that makes the reading possible, because it is about how English words are built.

The reading opens with something that happened to a real learner.
For two years she looked up every word she did not know, and she read very slowly.
Then a teacher wrote understaffed on the board. Nobody knew it.
So she split it. Under. Staff. Ed.
Everybody knew staff. Everybody knew that under means too little.
Four seconds later the whole room had it, and nobody had opened anything.
That is the first two patterns in this unit, and they are worth more to you than any vocabulary list.

Start with the negatives, because there is a piece of real system in there that learners are often told does not exist.
English has six ways of putting not at the front of a word. Un, in, dis, and the three that in turns into.
The prefix in changes shape to match the sound after it.
Before an l it becomes il. Illegal. Illogical.
Before an m, a b or a p it becomes im. Impossible. Impatient.
Before an r it becomes ir. Irregular. Irresponsible.
Everywhere else it stays in. Inaccurate. Incomplete.
That part is completely regular, and it explains something learners get wrong constantly.
Irresponsible has two r's, because the prefix keeps its r and the word keeps its r. Illegal has two l's for the same reason.
Now the honest half. Which of un, in and dis a word takes cannot be worked out.
Able takes un, so unable. But ability takes in, so inability.
Just takes un. Justice takes in. There is no reason, and no rule will help.
So learn which prefix, and let the sound rule handle the spelling.

The second pattern is the six prefixes that change a meaning rather than reversing it.
Re means again. Mis means wrongly. Over means too much. Under means too little. Pre means before. Out means better than.
All six are productive, which is a technical word meaning you can stick them on things and be understood.
Meet overstate for the first time and you do not need a dictionary. You know state, and you know over.
Two warnings. Over sometimes means simply above rather than too much: overhead, overseas.
And out has several jobs. Outperform is a comparison. Outlook and outbreak are not.
The technique does not always work. It works often enough to change what reading feels like.

The third and fourth patterns are the hard ones, and they finish something this course started in Unit 1.
Unit 1 taught you the small word an ADJECTIVE brings. Proud of. Keen on. Capable of.
Nouns do the same thing, and nothing before this unit has said so.
Information about. A reason for. A solution to. An increase in. Responsibility for. Confidence in.
There are two things about these worth knowing.
The first is that a noun and its own verb often take different prepositions.
You discuss something, with no small word at all. But you have a discussion ABOUT it.
So you cannot carry the verb's pattern across. They are separate items.
The second is the pair that sits together constantly and takes different words.
The cause OF a fault. The effect ON a batch.
Those two appear in the same sentence all the time and they do not match. That is just how it is.

Verbs are the fourth card and the biggest set.
Listen to. Depend on. Apply for. Consist of. Insist on. Cope with. Result in.
But the trouble is not the verbs that take one. It is the verbs that take NONE, because in most other languages they do.
You discuss something. You answer a question. You phone somebody. You enter a room.
Not discuss about, not answer to, not phone to, not enter into.
And there is one verb that changes direction depending on the preposition.
The delay resulted IN a loss. The loss resulted FROM the delay.
Same verb, same facts, opposite direction.

The last pattern is where formal written English gets its density.
In Unit 2 you put a plain -ing form at the front of a sentence. Learning a language takes years.
That form can carry two more things.
Being plus a past participle makes it passive. It happened to you. Being told late was the worst part.
Having plus a past participle makes it earlier. It happened first. Having finished the report, I left.
And both together: having been told nothing, we assumed it was cancelled.
Each of those replaces a whole clause with a phrase, which is why reports are written this way.
There is one rule that keeps it safe and it is not optional.
The phrase and the main clause must share a subject.
Having finished the report, I found the office locked is correct.
Having finished the report, the office was locked says the office wrote the report.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

grammar.title: Un-, dis-, in-, im-, il-, ir-: which negative prefix goes where
grammar.explanation:
English has six ways to say not at the front of a word, and they are not
interchangeable. Each word takes one and only one, and using the wrong one
produces a word nobody recognises.
Most of the choice is decided by the SOUND that follows.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IN- is the base form, and it CHANGES to match the next sound:
il- before l     illegal, illegible, illogical
im- before m b p impossible, imbalance, impatient
ir- before r     irregular, irrelevant, irresponsible
in- before the rest  inaccurate, incomplete, invisible
That part is predictable, and it is the only part that is.

UN- is the commonest, and it attaches to plain English words:
unable, unhappy, unfair, unknown, unwilling

DIS- reverses rather than negates, and often attaches to verbs:
dishonest, disagree, disconnect, dislike, disappear

Which of the three a word takes is NOT predictable:
unable, but inability
unjust, but injustice
There is no rule. Those are learned as items.

The useful half: once you know a word takes in-, the l, m, b, p and r
rule tells you its exact shape without being told.

grammar.explanation:
Six more prefixes, and these do not make a word negative.
They change what it says, and every one of them is productive: you can
attach it to words you have never met it on, and be understood.
That is what makes them worth more than a vocabulary list.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
RE-    again          rewrite, rebuild, reconsider, reissue
MIS-   wrongly        misread, misjudge, mislead, misquote
OVER-  too much       overestimate, overcharge, overload, overstate
UNDER- too little     underestimate, undercharge, understate
PRE-   before         preview, precaution, predict, prearrange
OUT-   better than    outperform, outlast, outnumber

The third and fourth are a genuine pair:
We overestimated how long the parts would last.
I underestimated how long the job would take.

Two traps.
OVER- sometimes means simply above: overhead, overseas.
OUT- has several jobs; better than is only one.
outperform is a comparison. outbreak and outlook are not.

Where this pays is reading. You meet overstate for the first time and you
need no dictionary, because you know state and you know over-.

an answer TO          an increase IN      a demand FOR

an attitude TO        a difference BETWEEN  an advantage OVER
responsibility FOR    an alternative TO     a reference TO

FIRST: the noun and its verb often take DIFFERENT prepositions.
to depend ON something  ->  a dependence ON it     (same)
to discuss something    ->  a discussion ABOUT it  (the verb takes none)

constantly.

This is the third and last source of these fixed pairs. Adjectives were

Verbs that MUST take one:
listen TO      depend ON      apply FOR      belong TO
consist OF     result IN      refer TO       object TO
insist ON      succeed IN     rely ON        deal WITH
cope WITH      complain ABOUT  concentrate ON  apologise FOR

discuss it     NOT discuss about it
enter the room NOT enter into the room
answer the question  NOT answer to the question
phone her      NOT phone to her
reach the site NOT reach to the site
lack money     NOT lack of money (as a verb)

result FROM  = is caused by  The loss resulted from the delay.

grammar.title: Being told, having finished: an -ing form with a voice and a time
grammar.explanation:
Unit 2 put a plain -ing form at the front of a sentence as its subject.
Learning a language takes years.
That form can carry two more things, and once it does it replaces a whole
clause. This is where formal written English gets its density.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
PASSIVE — being + the past participle. It happens TO you.
Being told late was the worst part.
She objected to being moved without notice.
Compare: telling her was the worst part. (you did it)
         being told was the worst part.  (it was done to you)

PERFECT — having + the past participle. It happened EARLIER.
Having finished the report, I left.
Having been told twice, he should have known.
The perfect says this came first, and the main clause came after.

BOTH TOGETHER — having been + the past participle:
Having been told nothing, we assumed it was cancelled.

Where each one goes:
as a subject       Being told late was the worst part.
after a preposition She objected to being moved.
at the front        Having finished, I left.

The rule that makes them safe: the -ing phrase and the main clause must
share a subject. Break that and the sentence says something absurd.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Make one sentence: I had finished the report. Then I left.
1. Which happened first? Finishing the report.
2. Earlier takes the perfect -ing: having finished.
3. Check the subject. Who finished, and who left? I did both.
4. Same subject, so the phrase is safe to attach.
Answer: Having finished the report, I left.
If somebody ELSE had left, this sentence could not be used at all.
grammar.commonMistake:
If the two halves have different subjects, the sentence attaches the action
to the wrong person. This is called a dangling participle.
No: Having finished the report, the office was locked.
That says the OFFICE finished the report.
Yes: Having finished the report, I found the office locked.
grammar.memoryTip: Being = it happened to you. Having = it happened first. Both need the same subject as the main clause.

assignments.title: The specification, and the words inside it
assignments.instructions:
Part one. Write a post specification for a job you invent, in about 150 words,
with a Purpose, four Essential items, two Desirable items and three Notes.
Every Essential item must be built on a noun that brings its own preposition.
Use at least three compound nouns and at least three prefixed words.
At least one Note must begin with Being or Having.
Part two. Pick any five words from your own specification that are BUILT from parts.
For each one, write the parts and say what somebody who had never seen it could work out.
Part three. Write five sentences about the post using these verbs, with the right
preposition or none at all: discuss, depend, apply, result, cope.
Then record part one aloud, and listen for the stress on your compound nouns.
